---
title: "Panel models"
subtitle: "Repeated observations of the same people: random-effects logit"
---
<<dd_version: 2>>

`mecompare` works after panel models such as `xtlogit`. The example uses the
Health and Retirement Study, 2010 to 2020: about 104,000 interviews of 26,000
people aged 51 and older, interviewed every two years. The outcome is
depressive symptoms (four or more of the eight CES-D items).

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/hrs_si_2025", clear
keep if year >= 2010 & age >= 51
generate depressed = cesd >= 4 if !missing(cesd)
generate poorhealth = srhealthB == 0 if !missing(srhealthB)
drop if missing(depressed, poorhealth, marstatB, age, woman, race4cat, collegeB)
xtset hhidpn year

quietly xtlogit depressed i.marstatB c.age i.woman i.race4cat i.collegeB, re intpoints(60)
estimates store dep
<</dd_do>>
```

After `xtlogit, re`, the marginal effects are changes in the probability of
the outcome, averaged over the random effect (the default prediction of
`margins`). Age is changed by ten years:

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
mecompare, models(dep) amount(10)
<</dd_do>>
```

Being married is associated with a 9.0 percentage point reduction in the
probability of depressive symptoms. Ten more years of age are associated with
a 1.2 point reduction, and a college degree with a 7.0 point reduction.

## Comparing two outcomes

The second model predicts fair or poor self-rated health. With two panel
models, `mecompare` combines them with [`suest2`](../../suest2/index.html),
which clusters the standard errors on the panel identifier. Random-effects
models need enough integration points to be combined; these two need
`intpoints(60)`, and `mecompare` says when a model needs more.

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
quietly xtlogit poorhealth i.marstatB c.age i.woman i.race4cat i.collegeB, re intpoints(60)
estimates store health

mecompare, models(dep health) amount(10)
<</dd_do>>
```

Being married is associated with a larger reduction in the probability of
depressive symptoms (9.0 percentage points) than in the probability of fair or
poor health (5.7 points); the difference of 3.4 points has p < .001. Age and
gender go in opposite directions for the two outcomes: ten more years of age
are associated with a 1.2 point reduction in depressive symptoms but a 3.5
point increase in fair or poor health, and women are 3.9 points more likely
than men to report depressive symptoms but 1.2 points less likely to report
fair or poor health.

A random-effects model mixes differences between people with changes within a
person. The [within-person effects](within-person.html) example separates
them.
